query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a small amount of yttrium (Y) into boride‐based components will promote the formation of a compact, stable oxide scale that resists molten‐aluminum attack during hot-dip plating.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional boride-based component (e.g. a metal diboride) without any rare-earth doping.
generation.intervention: Introduce a low-level yttrium dopant into the surface or bulk composition via alloying or surface treatment.
generation.conditions: Exposure to molten aluminum during hot-dip plating (temperatures around or above 660 °C) under typical plating atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent, Y-enhanced oxide (most likely an alumina or Y–aluminate) scale on the surface.
generation.mechanism: Yttrium is known to promote the nucleation and adhesion of protective oxide films. In this context, Y facilitates the formation of a self-healing, diffusion‐limiting oxide layer that slows down the dissolution of the underlying boride and reduces the attack by molten aluminum.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to non-doped boride components, Y-doped components will show reduced corrosion rates, lower weight loss, and improved surface integrity after molten-aluminum exposure.
generation.baseline: Performance of standard boride-based components (without Y) under identical hot-dip aluminum-plating conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only within an optimal yttrium concentration range; excessive Y content or extreme molten-aluminum environments with additional aggressive impurities may not yield further improvements.
generation.uncertainty: The exact doping level required and long-term stability of the Y-enhanced oxide scale under cyclic thermal or mechanical stress remains to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of identical boride-based samples: one set with a low-level yttrium dopant and one set without doping. Subject both sets to a controlled hot-dip aluminum plating process at ~660 °C for an extended period, then remove and clean the samples.
measurements: Weight loss measurement to quantify corrosion rates
Surface and cross-sectional analysis using SEM/EDS and XRD to evaluate the formation and continuity of protective oxide scales
Microhardness and mechanical integrity tests after molten-aluminum exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the yttrium-doped samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in weight loss, improved integrity of the oxide scale, and better preservation of mechanical properties relative to the undoped control samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively. The oxide scale morphologies of the coatings are shown in Figure 10c,g and the EDS analysis is shown in Table 4. It can be concluded that the oxidation corrosion products of the coatings were mainly Al-rich oxides. Additionally, there was also a certain amount of FeCr-rich oxides. Combined with the XRD results in Figure 9, it can be concluded that the corrosion product was mainly Al2O3. By analyzing the morphology and EDS of the corroded areas, it can be concluded that the elemental depletion of the EHEA coating was faster than that of the YHf coating, and trace amounts of sulfur elements were detected in the corroded areas of the EHEA. In conclusion, all coatings exhibited the same corrosion mechanism. The YHf-EHEA coating showed better resistance to the 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts hot corrosion than the EHEA coating at 900 °C.
